title: Sorting animals: by body covering, by legs and by food

summary.text: A hen and a crow both have feathers and two legs, so they go in one group. A hen and a cow have different coverings and different legs. You can sort animals by their body covering, by their legs and by what they eat. Covering and legs show at a glance, but to find an animal's food you have to watch them. Your child sorts the same animal cards three ways, compares two animals in overlapping hoops, and then puts out banana, rice and a dead insect to find out what the ants at home eat.
summary.art: A girl kneeling by a white paper on a kitchen floor, watching small ants walk to a piece of banana and a dead mosquito.

intro.hook: Stroke your arm and feel the tiny hairs. Now think of a crow and a fish. What covers each body? Then the harder question: what do the ants in our kitchen eat?
intro.text: Hair, feathers and scales are easy to see. Legs are easy to count. But you cannot see what an animal eats by looking at their body. Ask your child how we could find out what the ants eat, and let them guess. Don't give the answer. In this unit we sort animals by covering, by legs and by food, and then we test the ants.
intro.art: A boy stroking the hairs on his arm, with small drawings beside him of a crow's feathers, a fish's scales and an ant.

outcomes: By the end I can sort animals by their body covering: hair or fur, feathers, scales, a hard shell or case, or bare skin.
By the end I can sort animals by their legs: no legs, 2, 4, 6, 8 or many.
By the end I can sort animals by food into plant-eaters, meat-eaters and animals who eat both.
By the end I can say one way two animals are similar and one way they are different.
By the end I can say that one animal sits in different groups under different rules, and that humans are animals too.
By the end I can find out what an animal eats by watching, and say what I saw.

terms.meaning: A body covering is what grows on the outside of an animal's body, like hair, feathers or scales.
terms.example: Your body covering is skin with hair. A crow's covering is feathers.
terms.art: Three close-up circles side by side: human hair on skin, black crow feathers and fish scales.

terms.meaning: Fur is thick hair. Animals with hair or fur feed their babies milk.
terms.example: A cow, a dog, a bat and you all have hair.
terms.art: A calf drinking milk from a cow, with an arrow pointing to the hair on the cow's back.

terms.meaning: Feathers are light, soft parts that cover a bird's body. Only birds have feathers.
terms.example: A crow, a hen and a parrot all have feathers.
terms.art: A single grey and black crow feather lying on a window ledge.

terms.meaning: Scales are small, hard plates that cover the skin of fish, snakes and lizards.
terms.example: A rohu fish at the market and a snake on a wall both have scales.
terms.art: A close-up of a fish's shiny overlapping scales next to a snake's dry, patterned scales.

terms.meaning: A shell is a hard cover that protects a soft body. Insects have a hard outer case instead.
terms.example: A snail carries a shell. A tortoise has a shell too.
terms.art: A snail on a wet leaf and a star tortoise with a patterned shell.

terms.meaning: A herbivore is an animal who eats plants and plant parts, like leaves, grass, fruit and seeds. We can say plant-eater.
terms.example: A cow eats grass, and a parrot eats fruit and seeds. Both are herbivores.
terms.art: A cow chewing grass beside a green parrot holding a guava in one foot.

terms.meaning: A carnivore is an animal who eats other animals. We can say meat-eater.
terms.example: A gecko eats moths and flies. A tiger eats deer. Both are carnivores.
terms.art: A house gecko on a wall by a tube light, about to catch a moth.

terms.meaning: An omnivore is an animal who eats both plant food and animal food.
terms.example: A crow eats rice, fruit and insects. A crow is an omnivore.
terms.art: A crow on a ledge with a ball of rice and a dead cockroach beside them.

terms.meaning: Similar means alike in some way. Two animals are similar when they share a feature.
terms.example: A hen and a crow are similar: both have feathers and a beak.
terms.art: A hen and a crow standing side by side, with a tick drawn between their beaks.

terms.meaning: Different means not the same. Two animals are different when one has a feature the other does not.
terms.example: A cow and a crow are different: the cow has hair and four legs, the crow has feathers and two legs.
terms.art: A cow and a crow side by side, with a cross drawn between their legs.

explanations.definition: We look at what grows on the outside of each animal, and put animals with the same covering together.
explanations.description: Most animals have one of a few coverings. Hair or fur grows on cows, cats, bats and humans. Feathers grow only on birds. Scales cover fish, snakes and lizards. Some animals have a hard shell or a hard outer case, like snails, tortoises and ants. Frogs and earthworms have soft, bare, wet skin.
examples: Hair or fur: cow, goat, bat, human.
Feathers: crow, hen, parrot.
Scales: fish, snake, gecko.
Hard shell or case: snail, tortoise, ant.
Bare wet skin: frog, earthworm.
explanations.context: This card is about the first way to sort: by what covers an animal's body.
explanations.art: Five small boxes in a row, each holding one covering: hair, a feather, fish scales, a snail shell and a frog's wet skin.

explanations.definition: We count each animal's legs, and put animals with the same number together.
explanations.description: Snakes, fish and earthworms have no legs. Birds and humans walk on 2 legs. Cows, cats, frogs and lizards have 4 legs. Every insect, like an ant or a butterfly, has 6 legs. A spider has 8 legs. A crab has 10, counting the two big claws. A centipede has many legs, in pairs.
examples: No legs: snake, earthworm, fish.
2 legs: crow, hen, you.
4 legs: cow, frog, gecko.
6 legs: ant, cockroach, butterfly.
8 legs: spider.
explanations.context: This card is about the second way to sort: by counting legs.
explanations.art: A row of animals from no legs to many: an earthworm, a crow, a cow, an ant, a spider and a centipede, with a number under each.

explanations.definition: Herbivores eat plants. Carnivores eat other animals. Omnivores eat both plant food and animal food.
explanations.description: You cannot see food on an animal's body. You find out by watching what they eat. A cow eats grass all day, so a cow is a herbivore. A gecko by the tube light eats moths, so a gecko is a carnivore. A crow eats rice, fruit, insects and scraps, so a crow is an omnivore. A human body can eat both kinds of food. Many people choose to eat only plant food and milk.
examples: Herbivores: cow, goat, parrot, fruit bat, butterfly.
Carnivores: tiger, gecko, spider, frog, snake.
Omnivores: crow, hen, ant, humans.
explanations.context: This card is about the third way to sort: by what an animal eats. It comes after the ant test.
explanations.art: Three plates: one of grass and fruit, one with a fish bone, and one with rice and a dead insect, each with an animal beside the plate.

explanations.definition: Each sorting rule makes its own groups, so one animal can sit with different animals under different rules.
explanations.description: Sort by covering, and the hen sits with the crow and the parrot, because they all have feathers. Sort by legs, and the hen sits with the crow and with you, because you all have 2 legs. Sort by food, and the hen sits with the crow, the ant and you, because you all eat both plant food and animal food. The hen did not change. Only the rule changed.
examples: Covering: hen with crow and parrot.
Legs: hen with crow and you.
Food: hen with crow, ant and you.
explanations.context: This card is about the card sort, where the same hen card moved to new groups.
explanations.art: A hen card in the middle, with three arrows to three groups: feathered birds, two-legged animals with a child, and animals who eat both.

explanations.definition: To compare two animals, we list the features they share and the features only one of them has.
explanations.description: A crow and a hen are similar in many ways. Both have feathers, a beak, 2 legs and 2 wings, and both lay eggs. They are different too. A crow flies far, and a hen flies only a short way, up onto a wall. Two overlapping hoops show this well. What both share goes in the middle. What only one has goes on that animal's side.
examples: You and a cow: both have hair, both feed babies milk. Different: you walk on 2 legs, a cow on 4.
An ant and a spider: both have a hard outer case. Different: 6 legs and 8 legs.
explanations.context: This card is about comparing two animals, as in the Same and Different Hoops activity.
explanations.art: Two overlapping hoops on a floor, a crow on one side, a hen on the other, and a feather drawn in the middle.

explanations.concept: Food groups are not always neat
explanations.definition: Most animals eat mostly one kind of food, with some of the other.
explanations.description: Many animals do not fit one food group neatly. Some are mostly one kind of eater, with a little of the other. Scientists still argue about where a few of them belong.
examples: A frog tadpole eats tiny water plants, but a grown frog eats insects.
A female mosquito drinks blood for her eggs, and also drinks flower nectar.
A red panda in Sikkim belongs to the same big group as tigers, yet eats mostly bamboo.

perspectives.explanation: Food groups are useful, but they describe what an animal mostly eats. Most animals eat a little outside their group.
Dogs come from wolves, who are carnivores, so dogs are carnivores who also eat some plant food.
Dogs have lived with people for thousands of years. Their bodies now digest rice and wheat better than wolves do, so dogs are omnivores.

explanations.context: This card is about animals who do not fit the three food groups well.
explanations.art: A red panda sitting on a branch in a misty forest, chewing a bamboo leaf.

explanations.definition: Animals sense food and choose what to eat.
explanations.description: Ants sense food with their antennae, the two thin feelers on their heads. They decide which food to carry home. A colony collects both kinds of food, because the young ants need protein to grow, and the workers mostly drink sugary food. Animals sense food and choose between foods, and many remember where good food is.
examples: Ants found the banana and the dead insect, and carried bits home.
A crow remembers the window where rice is put out each morning.

perspectives.explanation: Ants sense, choose and remember. A colony decides together what to collect, from what each ant senses.
An ant follows simple built-in rules, and the colony's choices come from many ants following those rules.

explanations.context: This card is about what the ants were doing in the ant test.
explanations.art: A close-up of an ant touching a crumb of banana with her antennae.

agreed.text: Among animals alive today, only birds have feathers, and every bird has 2 legs.
agreed.evidence: Every kind of bird scientists have found has feathers and 2 legs, even birds who cannot fly, like the ostrich.

agreed.text: Animals with hair or fur feed their babies milk.
agreed.evidence: A cow, a goat, a bat, a dog and a human mother all feed their young milk. Scientists call this group mammals.

agreed.text: Every insect has 6 legs as an adult.
agreed.evidence: Ants, cockroaches, butterflies, bees and houseflies all have 6 legs. Spiders have 8, so spiders are not insects.

agreed.text: Humans and many other animals are omnivores.
agreed.evidence: Crows, hens, ants and humans can all eat both plant food and animal food. Jane Goodall found that chimpanzees do too.

challenging.claim: A whale is a fish, because a whale swims and has fins.
challenging.who: A common idea, held by many scientists long ago
challenging.for: Whales live in the sea, swim and have fin-shaped flippers.
challenging.against: A whale breathes air, has a few hairs, and the mother feeds her baby milk. That puts whales with the mammals, like cows and us.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous mix-up: is a whale a fish?

challenging.claim: A pangolin is a reptile, because a pangolin is covered in scales.
challenging.who: A common guess by people who see a pangolin for the first time
challenging.for: The Indian pangolin is covered in hard scales, like a lizard.
challenging.against: A pangolin has some hair on the belly, and the mother feeds her baby milk. A pangolin is a mammal. One feature alone can fool you.
challenging.context: This card is about the Indian pangolin, an animal with scales and hair.

challenging.claim: A plant-eater never eats animal food.
challenging.for: Cows, goats and deer eat plants nearly all day.
challenging.against: Deer have been seen eating bird chicks. Food groups say what an animal mostly eats.
challenging.context: This card is about whether food groups are strict.

big_questions.q: You can count a crow's legs in one look. Why does it take days of watching to find out what a crow eats?
big_questions.hint: A crow's legs are there all the time. Think about when a crow eats, and what is around.

big_questions.q: A butterfly has wings and 6 legs. A fruit bat has wings and 2 legs. Are wings a good way to sort animals?
big_questions.hint: Think about what else the butterfly and the fruit bat share: covering, legs and food.

big_questions.q: A human body can eat both plant food and animal food. Many people choose to eat only plants and milk. Which food group are they in?
big_questions.hint: Is a food group about what a body can eat, or what someone chooses to eat?

big_questions.q: The ants ate the banana. Is the banana now part of the ants?
big_questions.hint: Think about how your own body grows from what you eat.

story.title: Revathi and the Window Crow
text: Revathi was seven. She lived on the third floor of a building in Coimbatore, with her grandmother, Paati. Her cousin Nikhil was five. He came over every afternoon after school.

Every morning, Paati put a small ball of cooked rice on the kitchen window ledge. Most mornings, a crow came for the rice. The crow had a grey neck and shiny black wings. Revathi called the crow Kaka.
One day Revathi's teacher, Miss Selvi, gave the class a job. "Make a chart of animals," she said. "Put the plant-eaters on one side and the meat-eaters on the other."
That afternoon, Revathi spread out her pictures on the floor. A cow, a goat and a parrot went on the plant side. A tiger, a gecko and a spider went on the meat side. Then she picked up the crow.
"Kaka eats rice," said Revathi. "Rice is a plant. So Kaka goes on the plant side."
Nikhil shook his head. "But I saw Kaka eat a cockroach yesterday! A dead one, on the ledge."
Revathi frowned. "Are you sure?"
"Don't guess," said Paati. "Watch. Write down what Kaka eats every day this week. Then you will know."

So Revathi made a little table in her notebook. On Monday, Kaka ate the rice. On Tuesday, Kaka ate the rice and then a piece of banana that Nikhil had dropped. On Wednesday, Kaka pecked at a dead cockroach by the drain pipe and swallowed the cockroach. On Thursday, Kaka flew down to the bins and came back with something white. "Bread," said Paati. On Friday, Kaka snapped up a moth that was sitting on the window grill.
Revathi read her table out loud. "Rice, banana, bread. Those come from plants. Cockroach and moth. Those are animals." She looked at her chart. "Kaka doesn't fit on either side!"
"Then your chart needs a third group," said Paati.

Revathi drew a line down the middle of her chart. At the top she wrote: EATS BOTH. She stuck Kaka there. "Animals who eat both kinds of food are called omnivores," said Paati. "Your teacher will like that word."
Nikhil had gone quiet. He was lying on his tummy by the window, looking at the ledge. "Revathi, come and see," he whispered.

On the ledge, the banana bit from Tuesday had a crowd of tiny ants around it. A little way off, there was another crowd, around a dead fly. Some ants were walking away from the fly carrying a tiny piece of wing.
"The ants eat both too," said Revathi. She found an ant in her picture pile and put the ant picture next to Kaka.
Nikhil sat up. "Where do I go?"
Revathi thought about it. "You eat fish curry at home. And rice. So you go in the middle." She looked at Paati. "But Paati never eats meat or fish. Does Paati go on the plant side?"
Paati laughed. "A human body can eat both kinds of food. I choose to eat plants and milk. Your Aunty in Kochi chooses fish every day. We are the same kind of animal, and we choose different food."
Revathi drew a picture of a person in the middle column. Underneath, she wrote: "Humans can eat both. Each person chooses."
The next day, Revathi showed her chart to her friend Shalini. Shalini's chart had only two sides, and her crow was on the meat side.
"My crow eats rice," said Revathi. "And bread, and a banana. And a cockroach and a moth. I watched for a whole week."
Shalini looked at the middle column. Then she took out her crow and moved the crow to the middle of her own chart. "I need a third side too," she said.
Miss Selvi saw the two charts and smiled. "How did you find out?" she asked.
"We didn't guess," said Revathi. "We watched."
story.note: The facts in the story are true: house crows and many kitchen ants eat both plant food and animal food, and many families in South India put out rice for crows. Revathi, Nikhil, Paati, Shalini and Miss Selvi are made up.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Revathi could see Kaka's feathers and count Kaka's legs at once. She found Kaka's food group only by watching for a week. Two groups were not enough, so she made a third. Then she learned that humans can eat both, and each person chooses.
ask: Why did Revathi first put the crow on the plant side?
What did Revathi do to find out what Kaka really eats?
Paati eats plants and milk, and Aunty eats fish. Why did Paati say they are still the same kind of animal?
art: A crow with a grey neck eating a ball of rice on a kitchen window ledge in a city flat.
A girl and a small boy on a floor, sorting animal pictures onto a chart with two columns.
A girl writing in a notebook while a crow on the window grill snaps up a moth.
Tiny ants around a piece of banana and a dead fly on a window ledge, with two children peering at them.
A chart with three columns, plant-eaters, eats both and meat-eaters, with a crow, an ant and a person in the middle.

games.title: Find My Group: a card game with three kinds of rule
games.players: 2 to 4 players, with a grown-up to start
games.context: This is a card game with 16 animal cards and 12 rule cards. A rule card is turned over, and players lay down every animal card in their hand that fits the rule.

items.b: Feathers. 2 legs. Eats both: rice, fruit, insects and scraps.
Feathers. 2 legs. Eats both: grain, worms and insects.
Feathers. 2 legs. Plant-eater: fruit, seeds and buds.
Hair. 4 legs. Plant-eater: grass and hay.
Hair. 4 legs. Plant-eater: leaves and grass.
Fur. 4 legs. Meat-eater: deer and wild pigs.
Fur. 2 legs and 2 wings. Plant-eater: fruit and flower nectar.
Hair on skin. 2 legs. A human body can eat both. Each person chooses.
Tiny scales. 4 legs. Meat-eater: moths, flies and other insects.
Scales. No legs. Meat-eater: rats, frogs and birds' eggs.
Bare, wet skin. 4 legs. Meat-eater: insects and worms.
A hard outer case. 6 legs. Eats both: sweet plant juice and dead insects.
A hard outer case, and tiny scales on the wings. 6 legs. Plant-eater: flower nectar.
A hard outer case. 8 legs. Meat-eater: insects.
Soft, wet skin and a hard shell. No legs, one wide foot. Plant-eater: mostly leaves.
A hard shell and scaly skin. 4 legs. Plant-eater: grass, fruit and flowers.

printables.title: 12 rule cards to cut out
items: A hard shell or a hard outer case

rules: Cut out the 16 animal cards and the 12 rule cards.
Mix the animal cards. Give each player 4 cards, name side up. If any cards are left over, put them in a pile.
Mix the rule cards and put them face down in a pile.
Turn over the top rule card and read it out.
Every player puts down each of their cards that fits the rule, and says why: 'My gecko has scales.'
Anyone can check a card by reading the back. A card that does not fit goes back to that player.
If you put down no cards and the animal pile still has cards, take the top card. If the pile is empty, just wait.
Turn over the next rule card. Everyone who has no cards left wins, and the game ends.
If all 12 rule cards have been turned over and nobody has finished, the player with the fewest cards left wins. Two players with the same number win together.

setup.art: Two small piles of cut-out cards on a floor mat: animal cards with pictures and rule cards face down.
setup.caption: 1. Deal 4 animal cards to each player. Put the rule cards face down.

setup.art: A rule card saying 'Feathers' turned over, with a girl laying down a crow card and a hen card.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over a rule. Put down every card that fits, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Deal 4 animal cards to each player. 3. Put the rule cards face down.
flow.say: Each card is an animal. On the back it says the covering, the legs and the food. Each rule card is one way to sort.
flow.kid: Look at your 4 animals. Turn one over. What does the back say?

flow.do: Turn over a covering rule first, such as 'Feathers'. Each player lays down the cards that fit.
flow.say: The rule is feathers. Which of your animals have feathers? How do you know?
flow.kid: The rule is feathers. Put down every animal with feathers.

ask.q: A fruit bat has fur and wings. Why does the fruit bat card not go down for the rule 'Feathers'?
good: A bat has fur, not feathers.

flow.do: Keep playing. Turn over leg rules and food rules. Read the back of any card a player is unsure about.
flow.say: The rule is 'eats both'. Look at the back if you are not sure. Who eats plant food and animal food?
flow.kid: The rule is 'eats both'. Who eats plants and animals? Check the back.
flow.parent: The 'eats both' group is the crow, the hen, the ant and you. Children often put the cow there, because a cow gives milk. Ask what the cow eats, not what the cow gives.

flow.do: At the end, find the hen card and put the hen card on the floor. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: The hen fits feathers, 2 legs and eats both. Did the hen change, or did the rule change?
flow.kid: The hen fits three different rules. Did the hen change, or the rule?

check.q: Which rule puts the hen in the same group as you?
check.why: You and the hen both walk on 2 legs. The hen has feathers and you have hair. The hen eats grain and insects, so she is not only a plant-eater.

games.title: Three Clues: guess the animal
games.context: This is a guessing game. One player thinks of an animal. The others ask about the covering, the legs and the food until they guess.

printables.title: 9 question cards to cut out
items: Do you have hair or fur?
Do you have a hard shell or case?
Do you have more than 4 legs?

rules: One player picks an animal card from the 16 animal cards of the game Find My Group, and hides the card.
The other players take turns. Each picks a question card and asks it.
After each answer, the asker may guess the animal. A wrong guess counts as a question. A right guess ends the round.
Count how many questions it took. Then swap, so someone else hides. Try to guess in fewer questions than the round before.
Put the question cards back after each round. If all 9 are used and nobody has guessed, the hider shows the card and a new round starts.

setup.art: A boy hiding an animal card behind his back while a girl holds up a question card that says 'Do you have feathers?'
setup.caption: 1. One player hides an animal card. The others ask the question cards.

setup.art: A girl holding up three fingers and saying 'Gecko!', with question cards about scales, legs and food on the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Guess the animal from the answers.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the question cards. 2. The grown-up hides the first animal card, so the child sees how to play.
flow.say: I am thinking of an animal from our cards. Ask me questions. I can only say yes or no.
flow.kid: Your grown-up is hiding an animal. Ask the questions. Then guess.

flow.do: Play 3 or 4 rounds, taking turns to hide.
flow.say: Which question will cut the cards down the most? Feathers, or 'Do you eat other animals?'
flow.kid: Which question helps most? Pick it and ask.
flow.parent: A good first question splits the cards into two big groups, like 'Do you eat other animals?' About half the cards say yes. A question about one rare feature, like feathers, often gets a 'no' and tells less.

flow.do: Ask which question was most useful.
flow.say: Which question helped you most? Why?
flow.kid: Which question helped you most? Why?

check.q: The animal has scales and 4 legs. Which animal is this?
check.why: A gecko has tiny scales and 4 legs. A rat snake has scales but no legs. A frog has 4 legs but bare, wet skin.

experiments.title: Ant Lunch: do ants eat plant food, animal food, or both?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put three foods near the ants in your home: banana, rice and a dead insect. Then you watch which foods the ants come to.
experiments.question: Do the ants in our home eat plant food, animal food, or both?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the ants come to the banana, the rice, the dead insect, or more than one? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We put the three foods out at the same time, each the same distance from the ants. The pieces are all small. We count the ants on each food at the same times. If one spot gets all the ants, we swap the foods round on another day and try again, to check the spot was not the reason.

materials.item: a sheet of white paper or a steel plate
a piece of ripe banana, the size of your fingernail
a dead mosquito or fly (from a mosquito bat or the window sill), or a crumb of boiled egg or cooked fish
a tissue, to pick up the insect
a clock or a phone timer
a magnifying glass, if you have one

experiments.safety: Use the small ants of your kitchen, not big red ants, which can bite. Watch the ants, but don't touch them. Pick up the dead insect with a tissue, and wash your hands afterwards. Throw the food away at the end and wipe the spot.

schedule.what: Guess. Put out the three foods near the ants. Count the ants after 5 and 10 minutes. Say what you found.

experiments.record: Draw the paper with the three foods on it. Draw a dot for each ant you counted on each food after 10 minutes. Write P next to plant food and A next to animal food.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: ants on each food

setup.art: A line of small black ants walking along the edge of a kitchen counter near a wall.
setup.caption: 1. Find the ants. Look along the kitchen counter, the floor edge or the window sill.

setup.art: A white paper on a counter with three foods a hand-length apart: a piece of banana, five rice grains and a dead mosquito.
setup.caption: 2. Put the three foods on the paper, a hand-length apart. Put the paper a hand-length from the ants.

setup.art: A girl with a magnifying glass counting ants around a piece of banana and a dead mosquito, with a clock beside her.
setup.caption: 3. Count the ants on each food after 5 minutes and after 10 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the three foods. 2. Ask which are plant food and which is animal food. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason. 4. Write the guess down.
flow.say: The banana and the rice come from plants. The mosquito is an animal. Which will the ants come to? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Banana and rice come from plants. The mosquito is an animal. Which will the ants eat? Why?

good: Ants like sweet things, so the banana.
Ants carry dead insects, I have seen it.
They might like all of them.

flow.parent: Do not say what will happen. Every guess with a reason is a good guess. The test will answer it.

flow.do: 1. Find a place where ants walk. 2. Put the three foods on the paper, a hand-length apart. 3. Put the paper a hand-length from the ants. 4. Start the timer.
flow.say: Let's put the food where the ants can find it. Each food is the same distance from them. Now we wait and watch.
flow.kid: Put each food on the paper. Keep them apart. Put the paper near the ants. Start the timer.
flow.parent: Most Indian homes have small ants on a kitchen counter, a floor edge or a window sill. If you cannot find any, leave the paper near a window crack or the kitchen sink, and check every half hour. Start counting when the first ant arrives.

flow.do: 1. After 5 minutes, count the ants on each food and write the numbers. 2. Count again at 10 minutes. 3. Watch what the ants do at each food.
flow.say: How many ants are on the banana? On the rice? On the mosquito? What are they doing there?
flow.kid: Count the ants on each food. Write the numbers. What are the ants doing?

good: Pulling a leg off the mosquito.
Carrying bits away in a line.

flow.parent: Many kitchen ants come to both the banana and the dead insect, and fewer come to plain rice. Kinds of ants differ, so your numbers may be different. If almost all the ants went to the food nearest their line, do the test again on another day with the foods swapped round. If no ants came after 10 minutes, leave the paper and count again in one hour. Whatever you find is a real result.

chart.title: Made-up example: ants on each food after 10 minutes
chart.note: Made-up numbers to show what a chart can look like. Your ants will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they found, what they saw, and why. Then wipe up the food.
flow.say: Was your guess right? Which foods did the ants come to? So which food group are our ants in?
flow.kid: Was your guess right? Which foods did the ants eat? Which food group are they in?

ask.q: Which food group are our ants in?
good: Eats both, because they came to the banana and the mosquito.

check.q: In the ant test, ants came to the banana and to the dead mosquito. What does that tell you?
options: Ants eat both plant food and animal food
check.why: The banana is plant food and the mosquito is animal food. Ants that eat both are omnivores. If your ants came to only one food, try again on another day, because ants change what they collect.

activities.title: Who Sits With the Hen? Sort the same cards three ways
activities.context: In this activity you sort the same animal cards three times: by covering, by legs and by food. You watch which animals sit with the hen each time.

materials.item: the 16 animal cards from the game Find My Group
5 steel plates, bowls or sheets of paper, to hold the groups

setup.art: Animal cards sorted onto five steel plates on a floor: hair, feathers, scales, hard shell and bare skin.
setup.caption: 1. Sort all the cards by covering.

setup.art: The same cards sorted onto plates by number of legs, with the hen card next to a child's card on the 2-legs plate.
setup.caption: 2. Sort them again by legs. Who is with the hen now?

setup.art: The cards sorted onto three plates labelled with a leaf, a drumstick and both, with the hen, crow, ant and child cards on the 'both' plate.
setup.caption: 3. Sort them a third time by food.

flow.do: 1. Spread out the 16 cards. 2. Your child sorts them by covering onto the plates. 3. Ask who is with the hen.
flow.say: Sort every animal by what covers their body. Who is on the same plate as the hen?
flow.kid: Sort the animals by their covering. Who is with the hen?
flow.parent: Feathers: crow, hen, parrot. The butterfly has tiny scales on the wings and a hard case, so either plate is fine if your child says why.

flow.do: Mix the cards. Your child sorts them by legs. Ask who is with the hen now.
flow.say: Now sort them by legs. Who is with the hen this time?
flow.kid: Now sort by legs. Who is with the hen now?

ask.q: Who is with the hen now?
good: The crow, the parrot, the fruit bat and me.

flow.do: Mix the cards again. Your child sorts them by food, using the backs. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Now sort them by food. Read the backs. Did the hen change, or did the rule change?
flow.kid: Sort by food now. Read the backs. Did the hen change?

check.q: The hen sat with different animals each time. Why?
check.why: The hen card stayed the same. Each rule looks at a different feature, so each rule makes its own groups.

activities.title: Same and Different Hoops
activities.context: In this activity you make two overlapping hoops on the floor with dupattas or string. You compare a crow and a hen, then yourself and a cow.

materials.item: 2 dupattas, two long pieces of string, or chalk
small slips of paper and a pencil
the crow, hen, cow and 'you' cards from Find My Group

setup.art: Two dupattas laid in overlapping circles on a floor, with a crow card in one circle and a hen card in the other.
setup.caption: 1. Make two overlapping hoops. Put the crow card in one and the hen card in the other.

setup.art: Paper slips saying 'feathers', 'beak' and '2 legs' in the middle where the hoops overlap, and 'flies far' on the crow side.
setup.caption: 2. Put each feature slip in the right place: one side, the other side, or the middle.

flow.do: 1. Lay the two dupattas on the floor as circles that overlap. 2. Put the crow card in one circle and the hen card in the other.
flow.say: This hoop is the crow, and this hoop is the hen. The middle is for things that both of them have.
flow.kid: This hoop is for the crow. That hoop is for the hen. The middle is for both.

flow.do: Your child says features of the crow and the hen. Your child writes each on a slip, or you write it for them. Your child puts each slip in the crow side, the hen side, or the middle.
flow.say: Tell me one thing about the crow. Does the hen have that too? Then where does the slip go?
flow.kid: Say one thing about the crow. Does the hen have that too? Put the slip in the right place.
flow.parent: The middle can hold feathers, a beak, 2 legs, 2 wings, lays eggs and eats both. The crow side can hold flies far, and black and grey. The hen side can hold flies only a short way, and a red comb on the head.

flow.do: Clear the hoops. Now put the 'you' card and the cow card in the hoops, and compare again.
flow.say: Now compare yourself and a cow. What do you share? What is only yours?
flow.kid: Now compare you and a cow. What do you both have?

good: We both drink milk as babies.

check.q: Which feature goes in the middle for you and a cow?
check.why: You and a cow both have hair, and both drank milk as babies. Only the cow walks on 4 legs and eats only plants.

activities.title: Crow Menu: a week of watching (if a crow visits your window or balcony)
activities.context: In this activity you watch a crow at your window for a few minutes each day, and write down everything you see the crow eat.

materials.item: a small ball of cooked rice, if your family puts rice out for crows

schedule.what: Make a table with a column for each day. Watch the crow for 3 minutes and write what they eat.
Watch for 3 minutes. Write what the crow eats.
Watch for 3 minutes. Write what the crow eats.
Watch for 3 minutes. Write what the crow eats.
Read the table. Mark each food P for plant or A for animal. Which food group is the crow in?

setup.art: A crow on a balcony rail with a ball of rice, and a child watching from behind a window with a notebook.
setup.caption: 1. Watch the crow for 3 minutes each day.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of five days, listing rice, banana, a moth and bread, with P and A letters beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Write each food. Mark P for plant food and A for animal food.

flow.do: 1. Make a table with 5 columns, one for each day. 2. Watch the crow from the window for 3 minutes, and write what they eat. Your child writes, or you write for them.
flow.say: Let's watch quietly. What does the crow eat today?
flow.kid: Watch the crow for 3 minutes. Write what they eat.
flow.parent: Watch from inside, so the crow is not scared away. If no crow comes, a myna works too. Name the table after that bird.

flow.do: On days 2, 3 and 4, watch for 3 minutes each day and add to the table.
flow.say: What did the crow eat today? Was it something new?
flow.kid: What did the crow eat today? Write it down.
flow.parent: If the crow eats nothing in 3 minutes, write 'nothing today'. That is a real result. If you see only the rice, that is a real result too, but also write down anything else you see the crow carry off at other times of day.

flow.do: Read the whole table together. Mark each food P for plant or A for animal.
flow.say: Look at all the foods. How many came from plants? How many were animals? So which group is the crow in?
flow.kid: Mark each food P or A. Which group is the crow in?

check.q: A crow ate rice, a banana and a moth this week. Which food group is the crow in?
check.why: Rice and banana are plant food, and a moth is an animal. A crow who eats both is an omnivore.

projects.title: Our Home Animal Grid
projects.context: In this two-day project you make a big chart of the animals you can find in and around your home. For each one you fill in the covering, the legs and the food.

materials.item: a big sheet of paper or two sheets taped together

schedule.what: Draw a grid with 4 columns: animal, covering, legs, food. Fill in the first row for your child, then any animal you can see from the window.
Add the animals you found today. Colour each food box: green for plants, red for animals, both colours for both.

projects.record: The grid itself, with at least 6 animals, including a person.

setup.art: A big paper chart with 4 columns: a drawn animal, a covering, a number of legs and a coloured food box.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the grid with 4 columns.

setup.art: The finished chart with rows for a person, a crow, an ant, a gecko, a pigeon and a housefly, and green and red food boxes.
setup.caption: 2. Fill in each animal you found, and colour the food box.

flow.do: 1. Draw a grid with 4 columns: animal, covering, legs, food. 2. Fill in the first row for your child. 3. Add any animal you can see from the window.
flow.say: The first row is you. What covers your body? How many legs? What do you eat?
flow.kid: The first row is you. Fill in your covering, your legs and your food.
flow.parent: Animals that are nearly always about: ants, a housefly, a mosquito, a crow, a pigeon and a gecko. A mosquito has 6 legs, like every insect.

flow.do: 1. Add the animals your child found today. 2. Colour each food box: green for plants, red for animals, half and half for both.
flow.say: Look down the food column. Which colour do you see most? Which animals are like you?
flow.kid: Colour each food box. Which animals eat both, like you?

check.q: On your grid, which animal has 6 legs?
check.why: A housefly is an insect, and every insect has 6 legs. A gecko has 4 legs, and a pigeon has 2.

challenges.title: Feed the Rescue Centre
challenges.context: This is a planning challenge. You plan the food trays for five animals at a small animal rescue centre.
challenges.problem: Dr Meenakshi runs a small animal rescue centre in Mysuru. Today she is caring for a cow, a shikra (a small hawk), a star tortoise, a crow and a green parrot. She has only three food trays. How can she fill the trays so that every animal gets food they eat?
constraints: Every animal must get food they eat.
Foods to choose from: grass, fruit, seeds, cooked rice, small pieces of meat, and insects.
materials: the crow, cow, parrot and star tortoise cards from Find My Group, if you have them. Draw the hawk yourself.
general: Make one tray for each food group: a plant tray, a meat tray, and a tray with both.
Put the cow, the tortoise and the parrot at the plant tray, the shikra at the meat tray, and the crow at the tray with both.
creative: The crow eats both, so the crow could share the plant tray and the meat tray. Then the third tray can hold water.
Draw the food on each tray as a picture label, so a helper who cannot read knows which tray is which.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your three trays and the food on each one. Draw lines from each animal to their tray. Then add a new animal, a gecko, and say which tray the gecko needs.

setup.art: Five animals in a row at a rescue centre: a cow, a small grey hawk, a star tortoise, a crow and a green parrot.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the five animals. What does each one eat?

setup.art: Three drawn trays: one with grass, fruit and seeds, one with meat pieces, and one with rice and insects, with lines to each animal.
setup.caption: 2. Draw three trays and the food on each. Draw a line from each animal to a tray.

flow.do: Read the problem to your child. Show the five animal pictures.
flow.say: A small rescue centre has five animals and only three trays. What does each animal eat?
flow.kid: Five animals, three trays. What does each animal eat?

flow.do: Your child draws three trays, fills them, and draws a line from each animal to a tray.
flow.say: Which foods go on each tray? Which animal goes to which tray?
flow.kid: Draw three trays. Fill them. Draw a line from each animal to a tray.
flow.parent: A shikra eats lizards, small birds and mice, so the shikra needs the meat. A star tortoise eats grass, flowers and fruit. The gecko eats insects, so the gecko needs the meat tray. Let your child decide, and ask for a reason each time.

flow.do: Your child explains the plan. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Tell me your plan. Why does each animal go to that tray?
flow.kid: Say your plan. Why does each animal go there?

check.q: Which animal can eat from both the plant tray and the meat tray?
check.why: A crow eats both plant food and animal food. The cow and the star tortoise are herbivores, so they need the plant tray.

videos.channel: Dr. Jane Goodall & the Jane Goodall Institute USA

videos.check: Found by search: "Termite Fishing" by Dr. Jane Goodall & the Jane Goodall Institute USA, 2 minutes. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Getting to know pangolins

videos.check: Found by search: "Get to Know Pangolins on World Pangolin Day!" by Wildlife SOS, 1 minute 44 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: How crazy ants carry heavy loads
videos.why: Shows ants carrying food together, close up, so the child can compare the film with their own ant test.

quiz.why: Only birds have feathers, and a parrot is a bird. A fruit bat has fur, and a gecko has tiny scales.

quiz.p: Which of these animals is covered in scales?
quiz.why: A rat snake has dry scales. A frog has bare, wet skin, and a goat has hair.

quiz.p: An insect, like a cockroach, has how many legs?
quiz.why: Every insect has 6 legs. A spider has 8, so a spider is not an insect.
An earthworm moves by stretching and squeezing their body. A frog has 4 legs and a hen has 2.

quiz.p: A goat eats only leaves and grass. What is a goat?
quiz.why: An animal who eats only plants is a herbivore, a plant-eater.

quiz.p: A gecko by the tube light eats moths and flies. What is a gecko?
quiz.why: Moths and flies are animals, so a gecko is a meat-eater, a carnivore. Choosing 'eats both' would need the gecko to eat plants too.

quiz.p: Which is one way a crow and a cow are similar?
opts: Both have eyes and eat food
quiz.why: Both have eyes and both eat. Only the crow has feathers, and only the cow has 4 legs.

quiz.p: Sorted by legs, who goes in the same group as you?
quiz.why: A crow has 2 legs, like you. Humans are animals, and we share the 2-legs group with birds.

quiz.p: Sorted by covering, the hen goes with the crow. Sorted by food, who else joins them?
quiz.why: The hen, the crow and the ant all eat both plant food and animal food. A cow eats only plants and a tiger eats only meat.

quiz.p: Many scientists once thought chimpanzees ate only plants. How did Jane Goodall find out they eat animal food too?
opts: She read it in a book
She watched wild chimpanzees for months
quiz.why: Jane Goodall watched wild chimpanzees in their forest home. She saw them eat meat and termites. Food is found by watching, not by looking at fur.

quiz.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 2, wants to know what the ants in her kitchen eat. What should she do?
opts: Put out different foods and watch
quiz.why: You find out what an animal eats by watching what they choose. Legs and colour tell you nothing about food.

items.p: Sort these animals by body covering.
items.why: The cow and you have hair. The parrot and the hen have feathers. The snake and the fish have scales. The snail and the tortoise have hard shells.
items.art: Eight small drawings: a cow, a child, a parrot, a hen, a snake, a fish, a snail and a tortoise.

items.p: Draw a line from each animal to the number of legs.
items.why: An earthworm has no legs, a hen has 2, a goat has 4, a cockroach has 6 like every insect, and a spider has 8.
items.art: An earthworm, a hen, a goat, a cockroach and a spider on the left, and the numbers 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 on the right.

items.p: Colour the plant-eaters green, the meat-eaters red, and the animals who eat both half green and half red.
items.why: The cow and the goat eat only plants. The tiger and the gecko eat other animals. The crow and the hen eat both.
items.art: Six small drawings to colour: a cow, a goat, a tiger, a gecko, a crow and a hen.

items.p: Draw your ant test: the paper, the three foods, and dots for the ants on each food.
items.a: A drawing of the banana, the rice and the insect, with dots showing where the ants gathered.
items.why: A strong drawing shows all three foods, and shows clearly which foods had the most ants.

items.p: Every animal with feathers has 2 legs.
items.why: True. Only birds have feathers, and every bird has 2 legs, even an ostrich or a hen.

items.p: Circle the one who is not a plant-eater.
items.why: A tiger eats other animals, so a tiger is a meat-eater. The cow, the parrot and the goat eat plants.
items.art: A cow, a parrot, a tiger and a goat in a row.

items.p: Write or say one way a crow and a hen are the same, and one way they are different.
a: Same: feathers, a beak, 2 legs, 2 wings, they lay eggs, or they eat both.
Different: a crow flies far and a hen flies only a short way, or a crow is black and grey.
items.why: Any true shared feature and any true difference is a good answer.
items.art: A crow and a hen side by side, with two empty boxes underneath.

items.p: A friend says a bat is a bird, because a bat has wings. What would you tell your friend?
items.a: A bat is not a bird. A bat has fur, not feathers, and the mother feeds her babies milk. Only birds have feathers.
items.why: A strong answer uses the covering and the milk as evidence, not only a guess.

items.p: Two hens and one cat sit in a yard. Count all their legs.
items.why: Each hen has 2 legs, so 2 hens have 4. The cat has 4. 4 and 4 make 8.
items.art: Two hens and a cat in a yard.

items.p: Kavya and her sister Anjali are sorting animal cards.

views.says: Sort by covering. You can see it in one look.
Sort by food. Then you know how to feed each animal.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one way the other sister's idea helps.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and gives a reason. Covering is quick and needs no watching, which helps a bird watcher. Food tells you how to look after an animal, which helps a zoo keeper or a vet.
items.why: Both ways are good. Each one is better for a different job.

items.p: The Indian pangolin is covered in hard scales. A pangolin also has hair on the belly, and the mother feeds her baby milk. Which group is a pangolin in?
opts: Animals with hair who feed milk, like the cow
items.why: Hair and milk put the pangolin with the mammals, like cows, bats and us. The scales alone could fool you.
items.art: An Indian pangolin covered in brown scales, with a baby riding on her tail.

items.p: Sort these animals by their number of legs.
items.why: Snakes and fish have no legs. The crow and you have 2. The frog and the gecko have 4. The ant and the butterfly are insects with 6. The spider has 8.
items.art: Nine small drawings: a snake, a fish, a crow, a child, a frog, a gecko, an ant, a butterfly and a spider.

items.p: An animal who eats both plant food and animal food is called an ____.
items.why: Omnivores, like crows, hens, ants and humans, eat both kinds of food.

items.p: A frog tadpole eats tiny water plants. A grown frog eats insects. Which food group is a frog in? Why is this tricky?
items.a: A grown frog is a meat-eater, but a tadpole is mostly a plant-eater. It is tricky because the same frog changes food as they grow.
items.why: A strong answer notices that the frog's food group depends on their age, so one label does not fit the whole life.

items.p: Draw two overlapping hoops. One is 'has feathers' and one is 'eats both'. Draw a crow, a parrot and yourself in the right places.
items.a: The crow in the middle, the parrot only in 'has feathers', and the child only in 'eats both'.
items.why: The crow has feathers and eats both. The parrot has feathers but eats mostly plants. You eat both but have no feathers.

items.p: A plant-eater never eats any animal food.
items.why: False. Deer have been seen eating bird chicks. Food groups say what an animal mostly eats, not every single thing.

items.p: Which one of these has legs?
items.why: A frog has 4 legs. The earthworm, the snake and the fish have none.
items.art: An earthworm, a snake, a fish and a frog in a row.

items.p: Dr Meenakshi, a vet, and her nephew Farhan are talking about dogs.

views.says: Dogs are meat-eaters. They come from wolves, and they have sharp teeth.
Dogs eat both. Street dogs live on rice and chapati, and their bodies digest it well.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person gets right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with evidence. Dogs do come from wolves and have pointed teeth. But dogs digest starch better than wolves, and many live well on rice. Scientists still argue about this.
items.why: This is a real argument among scientists, so both sides have good evidence.

items.p: Mitali saw 3 crows and 2 dogs on her street in Kolkata. How many legs is that?
items.why: 3 crows have 2 legs each, which makes 6. 2 dogs have 4 legs each, which makes 8. 6 and 8 make 14.
items.art: Three crows on a wall and two dogs lying below them on a Kolkata street.

items.p: Write P for plant food or A for animal food next to each food from the ant test.
items.why: Banana and rice grew on plants. A mosquito is an animal, and an egg was laid by a hen.

applications: Zoo keepers and vets sort animals by food, so that each animal gets the right meals.
Bird watchers sort birds by feathers, beaks and size, so they can name the bird they see.
Farmers sort animals by food to plan their feed: hay for cows, grain for hens.
Scientists who find a new animal compare the animal's covering, legs and food with animals they already know, to decide which group the animal belongs to.

spotted.text: In many South Indian homes, a ball of rice is put out for crows in the morning. Crows come for it, and also eat insects and scraps.
spotted.art: A crow on a window ledge in Chennai, eating a ball of rice.

spotted.text: At a fish market in Kolkata, you can see the shiny scales on rohu and hilsa, and the hard shells of crabs.
spotted.art: Round baskets of silver fish with scales and grey crabs at a market.

spotted.text: Goats on a lane in Ahmedabad nibble leaves from a hedge. They are plant-eaters.
spotted.art: Two goats reaching up to eat leaves from a green hedge beside a house.

spotted.text: A house gecko waits by the tube light on many Indian walls at night, catching moths.
spotted.art: A pale gecko on a wall next to a glowing tube light, with moths around it.

open_questions.q: How does an ant colony know how much sugar and how much protein to collect?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that colonies with many young collect more protein. How the ants share this information is still being studied.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of insects are there?
open_questions.why_open: About a million kinds of insects have been named. Many more have never been found, and guesses of the total are very different.

ask_kids: What covers that bird's body? How many legs can you see?
At lunch: which foods on your plate came from plants, and which came from animals?
What do you think that crow on the wall will eat today?
Which animal at home is in the 'eats both' group with you?
If you could have any body covering, which would you choose, and why?

jokes.j: Why did the hen keep changing plates?
jokes.a: Because the rule kept changing, not the hen!

jokes.j: What do you call a spider who joins the insect group?
Why did the crow need a third basket?
jokes.a: Because they ate rice for breakfast and a moth for lunch!

jokes.j: What did the snake say when asked to count her legs?
Why do ants never go hungry at a picnic?
jokes.a: Because they eat both the banana and the fly that came for it!

jokes.j: Why did the goat refuse the fish curry?
jokes.a: She's a plant-eater. Leaves are her favourite dish.

jokes.j: Knock knock. Who's there? Omni. Omni who?
jokes.a: Omni-vore, and I'll eat whatever you've got!

jokes.j: What do you call a hen who counts her chicks?
Why does the gecko stay near the tube light?
jokes.a: Because the tube light is the only restaurant open all night!

maths.problem: Three ants walk onto the banana in the ant test. Each ant has 6 legs. How many legs is that altogether?
maths.explain: 3 groups of 6 legs: 6, 12, 18. So 3 ants have 18 legs.
maths.context: This is about the ant test, where ants came to the foods you put out.
maths.why_maths: Every ant has the same number of legs, so counting in sixes is faster than counting every leg.

maths.problem: In the ant test, Nandini counted 9 ants on the banana and 6 on the dead mosquito. How many more ants were on the banana?
maths.answer: 3 more ants were on the banana.
maths.explain: Count on from 6 to 9: 7, 8, 9. That is 3 more.
maths.context: This is about the ant test. These are made-up numbers.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two counts shows which food the ants went to more.

maths.problem: In the Same and Different Hoops, Lakshmi put 2 slips on the crow side, 5 slips in the middle, and 2 slips on the hen side. How many things are true of the crow?
maths.answer: 7 things are true of the crow.
maths.explain: The crow side and the middle both belong to the crow's hoop. 2 and 5 make 7. The hen side is not inside the crow's hoop.
maths.context: This is about the Same and Different Hoops, where you compared a crow and a hen.
maths.why_maths: In overlapping hoops, the middle counts for both animals, so you must add it to each side.

maths.problem: Jaya counted 12 legs in a picture of hens. How many hens are in the picture?
maths.explain: Each hen has 2 legs. Share 12 legs into twos: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. That is 6 twos, so 6 hens.
maths.context: This is about the hen card from Find My Group. A hen has 2 legs.
maths.why_maths: If you know how many legs each animal has, you can work out how many animals there are from the legs alone.

founder: ideas/by_topic/kinds-of-living-things-and-sorting-them.md: its notes are on climate zones and the story of life (fungi, sponges, comb jellies), which suit higher levels. Nothing fitted a Class 2 unit on covering, legs and food.
curriculum/sci.json: board chapter Cambridge Stage 2 4.1 'Comparing animals' (cambridge/sci-L2-04.json: comparing animals, mammals have hair or fur, birds have feathers, counting legs).
science: Only birds have feathers among living animals; all birds are bipedal.
Mammals have hair and feed young milk; whales are mammals with sparse hairs.
Indian pangolin (Manis crassicaudata): keratin scales, with sparse hair on the belly; mammal.
Fish scales (teleost) are made of collagen and calcium phosphate, a bone-like material; snake and lizard scales are made of keratin.
Adult insects have 6 legs; spiders 8; true crabs 10 including the claws. Centipedes always have an odd number of leg pairs, so never exactly 100 legs.
House crows and many household ants are omnivores; chickens are omnivores.
Worker ants rely mainly on carbohydrates, while ant larvae need protein to grow; colonies with more larvae collect more protein (for example Dussutour and Simpson, Current Biology, 2009).
Most frog tadpoles graze on algae and plant matter; adult frogs eat insects and other small animals.
Female mosquitoes take blood meals for egg production; both sexes feed on nectar.
Red pandas are in the order Carnivora but eat mainly bamboo; they live in the eastern Himalaya, including Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh.
Red deer on the Isle of Rum have been recorded eating Manx shearwater chicks (Furness, 1988).
Dogs carry more copies of the starch-digesting gene AMY2B than wolves (Axelsson and others, Nature, 2013); whether to call dogs carnivores or omnivores is argued.

Jane Goodall (born 1934) began watching chimpanzees at Gombe in July 1960, with her mother Vanne at first; late in 1960 she saw David Greybeard eat meat and fish for termites with grass stems. Before this, chimpanzees were thought to be mainly plant-eaters.
Bhagavata Purana 1.13.47: 'ahastani sahastanam apadani catus-padam... jivo jivasya jivanam'.
Taittiriya Upanishad 3.2: Bhrigu understands that food is Brahman; from food beings are born, by food they live, into food they return.
Many Jains avoid root vegetables, to harm fewer living beings in the soil.

roots.context: We have sorted animals by covering, by legs and by food. Now we ask what the ant test tells us about eating, and about where we fit.

deep_truth.truth: In the Ant Lunch test, the ants came to the banana and to the dead insect. So ants eat food from plants and from animals, like crows and most people. Animals who eat many kinds of food can find a meal almost anywhere. That is one reason ants, crows and people all live in our cities.
deep_truth.habit: We think of food groups as fixed labels, and we picture each animal with one kind of food. Many animals eat both, and these are often the animals who live closest to us.
deep_truth.evidence: In the ant test, the ants gathered on the banana and on the dead insect. Crows at the window eat rice, fruit, bread and insects. Both share our flats and streets.

three.who_am_i: You are an animal with hair and two legs, whose body can eat both kinds of food. You sit in many groups at once.
three.what_is_life: Every animal lives by eating other living beings, or what they made, like fruit and nectar. The ants on the banana were doing what you do at lunch.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of eaters, and each one chooses their food. A crow, an ant and a person can all find a meal in the same flat.

roots.thread: The banana grew on a banana plant, from sunlight, water and air. The ants ate the banana, and the banana became part of the ants. A crow may eat an ant, and one day the crow's body will feed the soil. So the energy that came from the Sun passes from one living being to the next.

teachings.teaching: Beings without hands are food for beings with hands. Beings without legs are food for beings with four legs. One living being is the life of another.
teachings.link: This old verse sorts animals by hands, by legs and by who eats whom, as you did with the cards. The ants and the mosquito showed its last line on your own paper.

teachings.teaching: The young seeker Bhrigu came to understand that food is Brahman, the one reality. From food all beings are born. By food they live. Into food they return.
teachings.link: Every food in the ant test came from a living being: a banana plant, a rice plant and a mosquito. The ants grew from what they ate.

science.text: In many kinds of ants, the young need protein to grow, and the workers mostly drink sugary food. So a colony collects both, and collects more protein when there are more young to feed.
How the ants in a colony share what the colony needs is still being studied.

other_view.view: Jain teachers say that living by other beings' lives is not something to simply accept. A person can choose to harm as few living beings as possible. Many Jains eat only plant food and milk, and many do not eat root vegetables, to spare the tiny beings in the soil.

practice.title: Where did my lunch live?
practice.say: Before you eat, look at your plate. Point to one food. Ask: where did this live before it came to me? A rice plant? A cow? Say it out loud. Now close your eyes. Breathe in slowly, and breathe out slowly. Then eat your first bite slowly.
practice.kid: Look at your plate. Point to one food. Where did it live before? Close your eyes. Breathe in and out slowly. Eat one bite slowly.

ask: What do you think a fruit bat eats at night, and how could you find out?
If you watched a crow for a whole year, would you see them eat something new? What might it be?
Why do you think some animals eat only one kind of food, and others eat almost anything?
roots.art: A child at a table with a plate of rice and banana, eyes closed, while ants carry a crumb on the window ledge behind.

how_we_found_out.context: Can you find out what an animal eats just by looking at them? This card tells the true story of a woman who watched and found out.
how_we_found_out.story: Before 1960, most scientists thought chimpanzees ate only plants: fruit, leaves and seeds. Jane Goodall was 26, and she had no university degree. The scientist Louis Leakey sent her to watch wild chimpanzees at Gombe, by Lake Tanganyika, in what is now Tanzania. Her mother, Vanne, came with her for the first months. At first the chimpanzees ran away whenever they saw her. Jane went back every day and sat quietly. Slowly they let her come closer. Late in 1960 she saw an old male, whom she named David Greybeard, push a grass stem into a termite mound, pull it out covered in termites, and eat them. She also saw chimpanzees eat meat from a young wild pig. So chimpanzees eat animal food too. They eat both, like crows and like most people. Nobody had found this out from books. Jane found it by watching chimpanzees in their own home, day after day.
how_we_found_out.who: Jane Goodall, an English scientist who studied chimpanzees, helped at first by her mother Vanne
how_we_found_out.when: 1960, at Gombe in what is now Tanzania
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That chimpanzees eat only plants. By watching wild chimpanzees for months, Jane Goodall saw them eat meat and termites, so chimpanzees are omnivores.
how_we_found_out.art: A young woman with a ponytail sitting quietly in a forest, watching a grey-bearded chimpanzee poke a grass stem into a termite mound.

playtest: Walked through every game, activity and the ant test as a parent and a child in a flat. Find My Group could leave players stuck when the animal pile ran out (4 players deal all 16 cards) and had no end if nobody emptied their hand, so it now says what happens in both cases, and Three Clues now has a clear end and a goal. Fixed the rescue-centre challenge (a young calf drinks milk, so the animal is now a cow), the story and worksheet names (Shalini is now only the story friend), a crow week that can return nothing, and dogs, deer and the pangolin, which came back in too many places. Removed one worksheet question that repeated the ant test, two weak jokes (adding two real ones), and the odd-pairs centipede fact that is too hard for age 7 to 8.
